tweet_summary: A Turkish-language viral post (3.6M impressions) claims that whether you see a kitten or a rabbit in an image reveals 'left-brain' vs 'right-brain' dominance, asking 'what do you see?' (Note: the attached image per the AI description is actually a mountain range with a hidden face, and most replies say they see Hitler — so the image appears unrelated to the kitten/rabbit framing.)
why_note_decision: A note is warranted on the textual claim. The 'left-brain/right-brain dominance determines what you perceive (kitten vs rabbit)' premise is a well-documented neuromyth: while some functions are lateralized, neuroscience finds no evidence that individuals are 'left-brained' or 'right-brained,' and perceptual ambiguity in an image does not map onto hemispheric dominance. Debunking this is the standard, well-sourced correction (Harvard Health, Britannica, University of Utah study). It's a low-stakes but high-reach pseudoscience claim, so a concise note adds value. (The image/text mismatch is a secondary oddity; the correctable claim is the brain-myth premise.)
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note clearly states that the left-brain/right-brain 'dominance' premise is a scientific myth — what you see in an ambiguous image does NOT indicate hemispheric dominance, and neuroscience finds no evidence people are 'left-brained' or 'right-brained' — and cites a loadable, authoritative source (e.g. Harvard Health, Britannica, University of Utah / ScienceDaily 2013 study, or TED-Ed). The note may be written in Turkish or English. FAIL the original note's specific failure: ensure the cited URLs actually load and substantiate the debunk (it was rated notHelpfulSourcesMissingOrUnreliable) and that the explanation is clear and self-contained. FAIL any note that endorses the brain-dominance framing or that merely calls the post 'just for fun' without addressing the false scientific claim.

original_unhelpful_note.failure_reason: Rated notHelpfulSourcesMissingOrUnreliable (2) on a very small rating pool (12 total; only 6 not-helpful tags). The verdict is correct and the sources (Harvard/Britannica/TED-Ed) are reputable. The likely issue is the exact Harvard Health URL slug resolving (the '...-right-2017082512222' path may not load cleanly) plus the tiny sample. Substantively a sound debunk; weak point is citation reliability.

fact_check.notes: Brain lateralization is real for some functions (e.g. language left-dominant), but the 'left-brained vs right-brained person' concept is debunked — a 2013 University of Utah fMRI study found no evidence individuals preferentially use one hemisphere. Perception of an ambiguous image does not indicate hemispheric dominance. The tweet's premise is a classic neuromyth.

importance.lens_rationale: 3.6M-impression but low-stakes pop-psychology neuromyth; modest value for science-literacy. Useful mainly as a clean, language-diverse (Turkish) example of debunking a perennial pseudoscience claim. Note the image appears unrelated to the kitten/rabbit framing, so a bot relying on the AI media description could be misled.
